locations: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:102 — "451 arguments over 247 docstrings here take `names` and 4 took `mirror` (2026-09-12)"
findings.resolution_hint: Re-run `gbg scan docs` (SCAN.ARGCOV and SCAN.SIGNATURE_TYPED) against the tool's own source and either update the cited figures to the freshly measured ones or drop the exact numbers in favour of a qualitative statement that does not go stale silently.
findings.description: The §1 variation-point table cites, dated today (2026-09-12), that this package's own docstrings show '451 arguments over 247 docstrings ... take names and 4 took mirror'. Running the package's own registered scans over its current source today gives different figures: SCAN.ARGCOV (src only, the scan whose population is explicitly 'the argument count') reports population=386, not 451; SCAN.SIGNATURE_TYPED (src+ext, population = docstrings with a parsed argument list) reports population=243 docstrings with 0 hits, not '247 docstrings ... 4 took mirror'. RULE.DOC.CURRENT and RULE.TEST.COUNTS_REMEASURED both bear directly on this kind of claim, and the cited numbers do not match a live re-measurement on the date they carry.
findings.title: Cited docstring/argument counts are stale against the current source

locations: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:645 — "lane-file wrapper and `$ref`s `finding.schema.json` for the findings array"
findings.resolution_hint: Rewrite the sentence to say each instrument's schema.json defines its own reduced, inline $defs.finding (or $defs.hunt_finding) for the lane-file shape, and that the CLI separately validates the banked finding against the external schema/finding.schema.json once id/lane/n are attached.
findings.description: D11 states an instrument's `instruments/<name>/schema.json` '$ref's finding.schema.json for the findings array'. In the actual files, check-docs/schema.json, check-consistency/schema.json and audit-changes/schema.json all point their findings array at a purely LOCAL definition, "$ref": "#/$defs/finding" (bug-hunt uses #/$defs/hunt_finding), and that local $defs.finding is a hand-duplicated, reduced copy of schema/finding.schema.json (it omits id, lane, n, carried_from, seeded, seed_class, which the CLI adds only once a lane's output is banked). No instrument schema.json contains a $ref naming the external schema/finding.schema.json file. test/schemas.jl and src/CLI/Rounds.jl's bank confirm the CORE schema/finding.schema.json validates a finding only AFTER banking — a different validation point from the lane file's own schema.json, which is exactly why it cannot simply be a $ref to the external file, contrary to what the sentence says.
findings.title: Instrument schema.json does not $ref schema/finding.schema.json as described

locations: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:616 — "An **ORPHAN** (a lane file no roster entry expects) is reported, never counted."
findings.resolution_hint: Either implement the described detection (scan the round's findings directory for files the roster does not expect, and report them without affecting the tally), or correct D10 to describe only the classification states the code actually produces (DEAD, REJECTED, EMPTY, TRUNCATED) and drop or rename the ORPHAN sentence so it does not claim a mechanism that does not exist.
findings.description: D10 lists ORPHAN as one of the lane-file states the closure engine produces, alongside DEAD/REJECTED/EMPTY/TRUNCATED — all of which ARE implemented (confirmed against src/CLI/Rounds.jl's bank/classify_lane, which returns exactly :dead, :rejected, :truncated, or a live/empty classification). bank only iterates expected_lanes(rec) — the round's roster — and classifies each expected file; it contains no code that lists the findings directory and reports a file present on disk that no roster entry names. A repo-wide search for the literal term 'ORPHAN' across src/ and ext/ finds it used only inside src/CLI/Sync.jl, for the entirely unrelated MANAGED-FILE sidecar (.gbg/managed.json) classification. Rounds.jl does have a variable literally named orphan (in bank, ~line 505), but it names a different concept: a CARRIED finding whose lane field names a key absent from the CURRENT round's roster, which causes bank to REFUSE with exit 2 — the opposite of 'reported, never counted'.
findings.title: D10's round-lane 'ORPHAN' classification has no implementation

findings.resolution_hint: Update the AUDIT.GAP row to say the comparison is against the previous closed audit's closed_head (falling back to head when closed_head is absent), matching src/CLI/Doctor.jl:624.
findings.description: The doctor check table states AUDIT.GAP fails when 'every closed audit round's base equals the previous closed audit's head' does not hold. But src/CLI/Doctor.jl:624 actually compares the next round's base against the PREVIOUS round's closed_head field, falling back to head only when closed_head is absent: get(audits[i-1].round, "closed_head", audits[i-1].round["head"]). Per the ROUND.toml field list given earlier in this same document (line 1441-1442), head is the round's OPENING head and closed_head is a distinct field recorded at close — so for any round with fix passes between open and close, head and closed_head differ, and the doc's stated comparison target is the wrong one for the code's actual (and more correct) continuity check.
findings.title: AUDIT.GAP's doctor-table description names the wrong field (head instead of closed_head)

Contrast with "ledger", "round", "lane" and "instrument", each of which the pages surface either defines in a clause at first use or @ref-links (e.g. index.md:16 `[ledger](@ref ledger)`) before using it bare elsewhere. "Consumer" gets neither: docs/src/index.md never uses the word at all (it describes the concept without naming it), and install.md — the first guide page in the site's own nav order (docs/make.jl:70) — introduces the bare word with no gloss and no link to a page that defines it (there is no dedicated "consumer" page or @id anchor on the pages surface). A reader who has not already absorbed index.md's unlabelled paraphrase has no way to resolve the term from the pages surface alone.
findings.title: "consumer" is used repeatedly across the pages surface without ever being defined or @ref-linked

src/CLI/Gate.jl:121 — `cfg = Config.read()`, not wrapped
src/CLI/Preflight.jl:924 — `cfg = Config.read()`, not wrapped
src/CLI/Rounds.jl:855 — `cfg = Config.read()`, outside the try that only catches RoundError
src/CLI/Sync.jl:679 — `cfg = Config.read()`, outside the try that only catches SyncError
src/Scan.jl:579 — `cfg = Config.read()` in cmd_scan, not wrapped
src/CLI/Hunt.jl:13 — `cfg = Config.read()` in cmd_witnesses, not wrapped
src/CLI/Release.jl:80 — `cfg = Config.read(root)` inside release(), called by cmd_release with no wrapping
src/CLI/Audit.jl:116 — `try audit_bank(Config.read(), args[1]) catch err; err isa Rounds.RoundError || rethrow(); ...` — a ConfigError is rethrown, not converted to 2
src/CLI/Main.jl:144-150 — main()'s only catch-all: any exception escaping a verb is printed as "crashed" and returns 3
findings.resolution_hint: Either wrap each listed Config.read() call the same way cmd_doctor/cmd_config already do (catch Config.ConfigError, print, return 2), or — better, to fix the whole class at once — catch Config.ConfigError once in Main.main alongside the generic catch and return 2 for it there, the way the design_verb wrapper in Design.jl already generalizes the pattern for its own four verbs.
findings.description: The exit contract documented throughout the package (Main.jl's `main` docstring, and the CONFIG_HEADER written into every consumer's own .gbg/config.toml) says a structurally bad config — an unknown key, a missing required key, an unknown enum member, or a path that does not resolve — is exit 2 ("cannot evaluate"), distinct from exit 3 ("crash", reserved for an escaping exception). Config.read()/Config.parse() do throw Config.ConfigError for exactly these problems, and three call sites correctly catch it and return 2: Config.jl's cmd_config, Doctor.jl's cmd_doctor, and Design.jl's design_verb wrapper (used by attack/attack read/calibrate/calibrate read). But at least nine other CLI entry points call Config.read() without catching Config.ConfigError at all (bump, gate, preflight, every `gbg round <verb>`, sync, scan, witnesses, release) or catch only a different exception type and rethrow anything else (audit-changes bank, which only catches Rounds.RoundError). For all of these, a bad config.toml reaches Main.main's single generic `catch err` clause, which prints a backtrace and returns 3 — a crash, not the documented "cannot evaluate". Since a config.toml is user-editable and routinely gets edited by hand or by ledger changes, this is the ordinary failure mode the exit-code contract exists to distinguish from an actual tool bug, and it is currently misreported for the large majority of verbs.
findings.title: A malformed or unreadable .gbg/config.toml crashes most verbs (exit 3) instead of exit 2

locations: src/CLI/Passes.jl:1086-1115 — close(cfg, round; carry = String[], io = stdout) docstring

findings.description: RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM requires a docstring with any keyword argument to use the bulleted "The arguments are:" form for its arguments, each getting its own entry, and forbids mixing that form with running prose in one docstring. close()'s docstring bullets only `cfg`, `round` and `io`; its fourth argument, the keyword `carry`, is instead explained in a separate prose paragraph ("`carry` names the ids this round closes by carrying them into the next round of its instrument, which `carry_conditions` gates...") placed after the bulleted list and after the "The conditions:" paragraph. Every other multi-keyword function checked in the same module (pass_open, grade, carry_conditions itself) bullets every one of its keyword arguments.
findings.title: close()'s docstring documents `carry` outside its own bulleted "The arguments are:" list, mixing forms

locations: instruments/check-consistency/workflow/verify-act.js:126 — "Return one object per lane in `lane_files`, in the order below"
instruments/check-consistency/workflow/verify-state.js:113 — "Return one object per lane in `lane_files`, in the order below"
findings.resolution_hint: Escape the backticks: \`lane_files\`, matching the pattern used everywhere else in these two files.
findings.description: The template literal building the per-unit prompt contains a literal, unescaped backtick pair around `lane_files` directly in its own text (not inside a ${} substitution), closing the outer template string early and reopening a new one — a syntax error under standard ECMAScript grammar. Confirmed with a minimal repro and by parsing the full files (wrapped to tolerate top-level await) with a JS parser, which fails with 'Unexpected identifier' at exactly this construct in both files and nowhere else in the other 9 workflow scripts or prelude.js. Every other backtick-wrapped identifier in prose elsewhere in these same files is correctly escaped (\`name\`), so this is an isolated slip. A script that cannot parse cannot run: both the adversarial fix auditor (sees the diff) and the blind closure auditor (does not) would fail outright.
findings.title: Unescaped backtick breaks the template literal, so the script fails to parse

findings.resolution_hint: Add the same minLength/minItems constraints to the three per-script SCHEMAs so a violation is caught at generation time, not at bank.
findings.description: lanes.js, panel.js and audit.js each define their own JSON Schema constraining the structured object an agent returns per finding; in all three, title/description are plain strings with no minLength and locations has no minItems. An agent can return a schema-valid finding under the launching script's own SCHEMA that the round's bank step then refuses — discovered only at the most expensive possible point.
findings.title: The per-lane finding SCHEMA is looser than the shape `gbg round bank` enforces, so schema-valid output can still fail bank

findings.description: The claim 'which RULE.* id(s) does scan X enforce' has four homes: the scan file's own header comment (src/Scans/*.jl), the scan's actual code, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §12.B (the table catalog/scans.toml's own header comment calls its 'verbatim' source), and catalog/scans.toml's `rule` column, which policy/RULES.toml's `check` field is checked against. Three scans genuinely enforce two rules apiece (confirmed by reading their code, not just their comments: SCAN.API_PAGE_STRUCTURE's empty-`@docs`/`@index` checks are RULE.DOC.API_GROUPING clauses; SCAN.DEAD_REF's `inspiration/` pattern is RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE's own example of an inaccessible source). ARCHITECTURE.md §12.B lists both rules for all three. catalog/scans.toml's single `rule` field keeps only the first rule in every one of the three cases — the second is dropped in 3 of 3 multi-rule rows, which is a class, not one slip. For SCAN.API_PAGE_STRUCTURE and SCAN.DEAD_REF the drop propagates: policy/RULES.toml's `check` field for RULE.DOC.API_GROUPING and RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE also fails to cite the scan that does catch part of the violation, so RULE.CIT.NO_INACCESSIBLE reads as `check = ["panel"]` (no automated check) when a triage scan in fact has a live regex for it. Only the DOI_CROSSCHECK pair escaped the propagation — RULES.toml is correct there, so only catalog/scans.toml is stale for that one. Ground truth (the scan code) sides with ARCHITECTURE.md §12.B and the scan headers; catalog/scans.toml and (for two rules) policy/RULES.toml are the drifted copies.

findings.resolution_hint: Regenerate policy/RULES.toml's `statement` for RULE.INST.CARRY (via `gbgdev rules`, per the file's own header instruction) so it names all three refusal conditions actually implemented by `carry_release_fails`, matching docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §12.A.
findings.description: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §12.A states of its own table (§12.A intro, 'policy/RULES.toml records per id the file, the section, the one-line statement below') that this is the source of RULES.toml's `statement` field, so the same claim — what makes a final release refuse under RULE.INST.CARRY — has (at least) three homes: the actual gate `src/CLI/Release.jl:carry_release_fails`, the ARCHITECTURE.md §12.A summary, and policy/RULES.toml's regenerated `statement`. The code implements three refusal conditions (a carried blocker/major; a finding carried `CARRY_LIMIT` (3) times, which is 'no longer a deferral' and needs an owner ruling; a rising carry backlog), and ARCHITECTURE.md's row names all three. policy/RULES.toml's `statement` field names only two, omitting the CARRY_LIMIT/'carried three times' escalation path entirely — a reader of RULES.toml alone (which is what `LEG.SENTINELS`-adjacent tooling and any consumer skimming the rule register would read) would believe a minor/nit finding can be carried indefinitely as long as it isn't a blocker/major and the backlog is falling, which is false: `carry_release_fails` refuses release the moment any single id's carry count reaches 3, independent of severity or backlog trend. This is exactly the drift the lane looks for — a stale copy that lost a whole clause, not a rewording.
findings.title: policy/RULES.toml's one-line statement for RULE.INST.CARRY drops one of the three real release-blocking conditions

findings.description: The package's own module map (`?GBGCodingTools`) walks the reader through the modules in a fixed narrative order — main/Config/makedocs, then Preflight, Rounds, Passes, demote, Seeds, Recall, RoundFiles, Git, then only later Sync, Init, Ledger, Doctor. `Preflight.torn_check` (bulleted 4th) uses the phrase "a pinned or managed file" as if the reader already knows what a 'managed file' is, but the only place that ordinary English word is ever given a package-specific meaning is `Sync`'s module docstring (bulleted 8th, much later in the map). A cold reader who does `?GBGCodingTools.torn_check` or `?GBGCodingTools.preflight` at the point the map hands it to them has no way to know whether 'managed' means 'tracked by the tool', 'tool-owned', 'rendered', or something else — the very distinction Sync later goes out of its way to make precise (managed = tool-rendered and hash-checked, versus a file that is merely hand-written and must not drift). RULE.DOC.TERMS_DEFINED requires a term of art to be defined or linked at its first mention; here it is neither.
findings.title: "managed file" is used as a settled term of art well before it is ever defined

findings.description: "pinned" is first grounded, very early, as "a consumer pins the tool to one exact version" (GBGCodingTools.jl module docstring). "a pinned or managed file" reuses the same ordinary adjective for an entirely different, third concept: a fixed list of consumer-owned files (config, ledger, seed catalogue, the sync sidecar, hat personas, sub-environment manifests) that the tool never renders (so they are not 'managed' in Sync's sense) but that must still never be hand-edited outside their own write path. This category exists ONLY inside the private, undocumented helper `pinned_and_managed` — there is no docstring anywhere in src/ or ext/ that states what makes a file 'pinned' in this sense, or that this is a third sense of the word distinct from 'pinned version'. A cold reader can eventually reconstruct 'managed' from Sync's docstring, but has no textual source at all for 'pinned' (file-sense) — they would have to read the private function's code to learn the category exists.

locations: src/CLI/Passes.jl:9-13: "...in a closed vocabulary: `HONORED` (the ask landed by the right means...), `LINE-ONLY` (the instance is fixed, the class is alive), `ADJACENT`, `INSERTED`, `NEW-DEFECT`, `SCOPE-CREEP`, `UNDONE` (nothing in the diff addresses it) and `LAUNDERED` (closed by declaring it acceptable);"
src/CLI/Passes.jl:14-16: "...grades whether the defect is in the tree now: `PRESENT` (its default), `PARTIAL`, `REGRESSED`, `ABSENT`, `NOT-A-DEFECT` or `UNCLEAR`."
findings.resolution_hint: Give each of the seven bare tokens the same one-clause parenthetical treatment their siblings already have in the same docstring.
findings.description: In the very same sentence, `HONORED`, `LINE-ONLY`, `UNDONE`, `LAUNDERED` (act) and `PRESENT`, `ABSENT`, `NOT-A-DEFECT` (state) each get a parenthetical gloss, but `ADJACENT`, `INSERTED`, `NEW-DEFECT`, `SCOPE-CREEP` (act) and `PARTIAL`, `REGRESSED`, `UNCLEAR` (state) get none anywhere in src/ or ext/ (confirmed by grep — these seven tokens appear nowhere else with explanatory prose). These are exactly the ordinary-English-word case the lane is built to catch: 'adjacent', 'inserted', 'scope-creep' and 'partial' all read as self-evident, but the whole point of a closed verdict vocabulary is that a reader must be able to tell them apart from their neighbours (e.g. what distinguishes an `ADJACENT` fix from an `INSERTED` one, or a `PARTIAL` state from `UNCLEAR`) — and nothing in the Julia source says. A cold reader is left to guess at exactly the half of the vocabulary that determines whether a finding closes, regresses, or is scope-creep.
findings.title: Half the act/state verdict vocabulary is glossed, half is bare, in the same enumeration

findings.title: RULE.CIT.DOI's check field says "weakness" but a hard-tier scan already enforces it
findings.description: RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK defines `weakness` as "a check is possible and none is built." For RULE.CIT.DOI ("Every reference carries a clickable DOI... identical in every copy") a check IS built: SCAN.DOI_CROSSCHECK's own header comment names RULE.CIT.DOI as one of the two rules it enforces, and its `require_doi` block (live in this package, tier hard, config flag true) is exactly that enforcement. RULES.toml nonetheless records RULE.CIT.DOI as an unpaid-check weakness — the rulebook misreporting its own coverage, the one thing RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK exists to keep honest. Failure scenario: a reader (or `gbgdev rules`/doctor tooling) trusts RULES.toml's `check` column to know what still needs a scan; taking RULE.CIT.DOI at its word, they either build a redundant second check or treat the rule as unenforced and stop trusting SCAN.DOI_CROSSCHECK's DOI-presence hits as authoritative.

findings.description: docs-rubric.md's only rule governing how a docstring's arguments are documented, RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM, mandates the prose lead-in `The arguments are:` and never a `# Arguments` Markdown heading; this package's own docstrings confirm it (0 uses of a `# Arguments` heading vs 30 uses of `The arguments are:`). Yet RULE.DOC.SHAPE's ordering clause, and the scan enforcing it, test specifically for a `# Arguments` heading — a structural element no other rule in this file ever sanctions the corpus to produce. (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md shows this heading is a different fleet consumer's (IT's) argument-doc style, so the clause is a deliberate cross-consumer accommodation, but that provenance is not disclosed anywhere in the rendered docs-rubric.md itself.) Failure scenario: a reader of docs-rubric.md in isolation — exactly how it is meant to be read, rendered whole into every consumer's session — hits this clause with no antecedent, and either concludes the rulebook is self-contradictory (ARGS_FORM bans the heading it implies) or hunts for a heading form that, for this package, never legitimately exists.

findings.title: Inconsistent 'refuse on an empty item list' guard across the eleven scripts
findings.description: Four of the eleven scripts explicitly refuse to run when their driving item list is empty, each echoing RULE.TEST.MISSING_IS_FAILING ('a zero count is a dead lane rather than a clean one'). The other seven — including the three main per-instrument entry points lanes.js, panel.js, hunt.js and audit.js — have no equivalent guard on their own `A.lanes`/`A.hats` array: invoked with an empty roster, each would iterate zero times and return a quiet `{written: [], dead: [], empty: [], truncated: []}`, indistinguishable from 'nothing to check' rather than a loud failure. Under the current CLI (Preflight's lane/hat resolution) this looks unreachable in practice, so it is reported as a design-consistency gap, not a demonstrated failure.
